According to "Ett grönare Kalmar", at least 45% is to come from the local area and 85% be organic or Swedish (82.0% in 2023). How the "local area" is delimited is not stated in the source. Applies only to public meals, about 12,000 portions per day.

svenska_livsmedel_kommunen.name: Swedish food as a share of the municipality's food purchases
svenska_livsmedel_kommunen.note: In 2024, 25% of purchases were organic and the climate impact was 1.6 kg CO2e per kg of food. The catering operation prepares about 12,000 portions per day. The share from the local area is not reported for 2024.

byggnadsminnen_kvarnholmen.name: Buildings protected as listed buildings (byggnadsminnen) on Kvarnholmen
byggnadsminnen_kvarnholmen.note: National interest H48 Kalmar: "Renaissance town with castle environment and fortification system". The expressions of the national interest include the grid plan, the stone houses from the 17th and 18th centuries, the silhouette with the Cathedral, the canals, the remains of ramparts and bastions and the sightlines to the castle. In the 2015–2016 revision the area was limited to the 17th-century environments, so that the city blocks on Ängö, parts of Malmen, Kalmarsundsparken and Stensö ended up outside (Swedish National Heritage Board press release).

byggnadsminnen_klimatrisk_lan.name: Listed buildings in Kalmar County at risk of damage from climate change by 2100
byggnadsminnen_klimatrisk_lan.note: 48 of 136 listed buildings; 46 of them are threatened by sea level rise. In the same GIS analysis, 24.9% of the q-marked buildings (622 of 2,497), 41.6% of the national interests (32 of 77) and 14.4% of the ancient monuments are affected. The scenario is RCP8.5: 1 m higher mean water level plus 1.5 m high water, i.e. 2.5 m. In Kalmar, the castle, the residence and the Klapphuset are in the risk zone.

kalmar_slott_besokare.name: Visitors to Kalmar Castle per year
kalmar_slott_besokare.note: "Latest annual statistics" in a 2025 issue; the year 2024 is assumed. The castle is a state-listed building owned and managed by the National Property Board of Sweden. The figure shows the castle's role as a visitor destination in the cultural environment threatened by rising seas.

op_planeringsniva_invanare_2035.name: Comprehensive plan's planning level: inhabitants in Kalmar Municipality in 2035
op_planeringsniva_invanare_2035.note: "The comprehensive plan allows for about 82,000 inhabitants in 2035." That corresponds to approx. +1.2% per year from 73,068 inhabitants in 2025, versus +0.5% during 2025. The comprehensive plan text itself gives no housing figures per area (consultation report 2022).

mal_fardigstallda_bostader_per_ar.name: Target: completed homes per year (five-year average)
mal_fardigstallda_bostader_per_ar.note: The municipal group is to contribute to at least 500 homes being completed per year and 50 new detached-house plots being made available each year. In 2025 about 70 homes were completed (0.96 per 1,000 inhabitants). A new housing supply programme is to be drawn up.

snurrom_friluftsstaden_kapacitet.name: Snurrom (the outdoor city): people who can live and work there at full build-out
snurrom_friluftsstaden_kapacitet.note: About 1,100 homes are already complete. The planning programme covers Krafslösa, Vimpeltorpet and Snurrom. The 2024 operational plan states that about 8,500 inhabitants can live there in the long term. It is the municipality's largest development area.

markniva_lagsta_gata_kvarnholmen.name: Lowest street/quay level on Kvarnholmen (Ölandskajen)
markniva_lagsta_gata_kvarnholmen.note: Own calculation: ground level = water level 3.4 m minus the map's water depth 1.89 m = 1.51 m; same result from the threat map for 2.7 m. Next come Skeppsbrogatan at Skeppsbron 1.6 m, Kaggensgatan (southern) 1.8 m, Södra Vallgatan, Elevatorkajen and Östra Sjögatan (northern) 1.9 m. Quay edges and steps may lie lower.

markniva_typisk_kvarnholmen.name: Typical ground level on Kvarnholmen (median of the land surface)
markniva_typisk_kvarnholmen.note: Own calculation: share of Kvarnholmen's 45 ha of land surface that MCF's coastal layer shows as flooded at each decimetre. 50% lies below approx. 2.7 m. The range gives the 25th–75th percentile, 2.1–3.7 m. 17% lies below 2.0 m. The highest part is Storgatan–Stortorget, approx. 3.9–4.4 m. The ramparts and bastions lie above 5 m and make up 2% of the area.

andel_kvarnholmen_under_2m.name: Share of Kvarnholmen's land surface flooded at sea level +2.0 m RH2000
andel_kvarnholmen_under_2m.note: Own calculation by pixel counting: 5% at 1.8 m, 17% at 2.0 m, 42% at 2.5 m and 57% at 3.0 m. The harbour area south of Kvarnholmen (Barlastholmen, Tjärhovet and the railway yard, 51 ha) is already 68% flooded at 2.0 m. The calculation assumes no protection and no waves.

hogvatten_100ar_idag.name: Sea water level with a 100-year return period in Kalmar, current climate
hogvatten_100ar_idag.note: That is 115 cm above the 1995–2014 mean water level, which is 14 cm RH2000. The range 122–136 cm is a 90% credibility interval. The value comes from a Bayesian model with 44 measuring stations, since Kalmar lacks a long measurement series. It replaces the model's assumed storm surge of 1.75 m.

hogvatten_500ar_idag.name: Sea water level with a 500-year return period in Kalmar, current climate
hogvatten_500ar_idag.note: That is 125 cm above the mean water level, with a 90% interval of 131–148 cm. The 50-year level is 123 cm (117–129).

hogvatten_100ar_2100_ssp245.name: 100-year sea water level in Kalmar in 2100 (SSP2-4.5)
hogvatten_100ar_2100_ssp245.note: Includes land uplift. 90% confidence interval 138–215 cm. The 500-year level is 186 cm.

hogvatten_100ar_2100_ssp585.name: 100-year sea water level in Kalmar in 2100 (SSP5-8.5)
hogvatten_100ar_2100_ssp585.note: Includes land uplift. 90% confidence interval 144–250 cm. SSP3-7.0 gives 185 cm (137–234).

hogvatten_100ar_2150_ssp245.name: 100-year sea water level in Kalmar in 2150 (SSP2-4.5)
hogvatten_100ar_2150_ssp245.note: 90% confidence interval 134–271 cm. MCF's 2026 threat map uses the upper limit, rounded to 2.7 m.

hogvatten_100ar_2150_ssp585.name: 100-year sea water level in Kalmar in 2150 (SSP5-8.5)
hogvatten_100ar_2150_ssp585.note: 90% confidence interval 142–339 cm. MCF's 2026 threat map uses the upper limit, 3.4 m. At that level about 64% of Kvarnholmen's land surface is under water without protection (own pixel count).

havsniva_hojning_2150_ssp245.name: Sea level rise in Kalmar to 2150 (SSP2-4.5, median)
havsniva_hojning_2150_ssp245.note: Net rise after land uplift: the mean water level goes from 14 cm (1995–2014) to 87 cm in RH 2000. The likely range (17th–83rd percentile) is 55–131 cm in RH 2000, i.e. a rise of 41–117 cm.

havsniva_hojning_2150_ssp585.name: Sea level rise in Kalmar to 2150 (SSP5-8.5, median)
havsniva_hojning_2150_ssp585.note: The mean water level becomes 126 cm in RH 2000 versus 14 cm in 1995–2014. The likely range is 80–187 cm in RH 2000, i.e. a rise of 66–173 cm. The 5th–95th percentile is 57–236 cm in RH 2000.

havsniva_hojning_2150_ssp585_mindre_trol.name: Sea level rise in Kalmar to 2150, low-likelihood high scenario (SSP5-8.5, median)
havsniva_hojning_2150_ssp585_mindre_trol.note: The scenario includes unstable ice sheets. The mean water level becomes 189 cm in RH 2000, with 80–488 cm as the 17th–83rd percentile, i.e. a rise of 66–474 cm. It is relevant as a stress test, not as a planning case.

hogsta_uppmatta_vattenstand_kalmar.name: Highest measured sea water level at Kalmar's measuring station (January 2012)
hogsta_uppmatta_vattenstand_kalmar.note: The Swedish Maritime Administration's Kalmar station has measured since 2009. According to SMHI's hourly data, the peak on 14 January 2012 corresponds to approx. 110 cm RH2000, but the value is not quality-controlled. The highest checked hourly value is 104 cm RH2000 on 2 January 2019. Oskarshamn's record is 115 cm above mean water level (4 January 2017) and Kungsholmsfort's 133 cm (January 1914).

medelvattenstand_kalmar_2024.name: Calculated mean water level in Kalmar 2024
medelvattenstand_kalmar_2024.note: Apparent land uplift at the Kalmar station is 0.06 cm/year for the measurement period, i.e. almost zero: the sea has in practice eaten up the land uplift. The mean of SMHI's hourly data 2016–2026 is approx. 17 cm (own calculation).

hamn_klarar_permanent_hojning.name: Permanent sea level rise that Kalmar harbour can withstand in its current design
hamn_klarar_permanent_hojning.note: The municipality's assessment: the harbour may need reinforcement against temporary high water even before then. The guest harbour is also severely affected if the mean level rises more than approx. 0.7 m. At 1 m, further protective measures are required.

bhn_idag_kalmar.name: Calculated highest sea level in Kalmar at present (BHN, no planning horizon)
bhn_idag_kalmar.note: The County Administrative Board considers that existing housing and critical societal functions should take into account risks up to this level already today. BHN with a 2120 horizon is 278 cm, rounded to 280 cm, which is the planning level for new development.

dricksvattenmarginal_kalmar.name: Drinking water margin in Kalmar (available raw water above demand)
dricksvattenmarginal_kalmar.note: Kalmar Vatten's own key figure for the ratio between available raw water and what society needs. At the end of 2024 the margin was 39 % ('overcapacity in water resources of 39 %', annual report 2024); in the dry year 2025 it fell to 19 % as wells outside the infiltration areas lost capacity. The report does not say whether the margin is based on annual volume or peak day.

ofakturerat_dricksvatten_andel_kalmar.name: Share of produced drinking water not billed in Kalmar (leakage, metering error, own use)
ofakturerat_dricksvatten_andel_kalmar.note: Non-billed water = 100 minus the billing ratio. It was 16 % in 2023 and about 9 % in 2025 (4,947,670 m³ sold of 5,437,000 m³ produced, own calculation), a cut of roughly 0.5 million m³ a year in two years. The national average for delivered volume without revenue was 22 % in 2024 (Svenskt Vatten, VASS).

hushallens_vattenanvandning_per_person_k.name: Household drinking water use per connected person per day, Kalmar municipality
hushallens_vattenanvandning_per_person_k.note: Own calculation: households' 3.9 million m³ a year divided by 66,000 connected people and 365 days. The national average is 140 l according to Kalmar Vatten and 135 l according to Svenskt Vatten 2024; households in the county used about 150 l (SCB 2020). The sector split in the source is rounded and its total (5.56 million m³) is higher than the volume sold in 2025.

hushallens_vattenbehov_2050_kalmar.name: Forecast household drinking water use in Kalmar municipality in 2050
hushallens_vattenbehov_2050_kalmar.note: Up from 3.9 million m³ a year today, with more residents and a higher connection rate; this corresponds to about 100,000 connected people at 140–150 l per person per day (own calculation). Cutting use by 15 % to 120 l per person per day would need only 4.5 million m³. The municipal water supply plan concludes that the municipality's water resources are not large enough to secure future needs.

oberoende_ravattensystem_kalmar.name: Number of independent raw-water systems for Kalmar's drinking water
oberoende_ravattensystem_kalmar.note: All production comes from the Nybroåsen esker: natural groundwater plus groundwater formed from pre-treated water from the river Hagbyån, topped up from a lake reservoir (Hultebräan lies within Hagbyån's protection zone); the wellfields are Hagbymassivet (Bottorp–Stenkällan), Vassmolösa–Ölvingstorp and Råsbäck, and the water is treated at Skälby waterworks. Desalination and recycled water are being studied but nothing is decided. The 2013 regional plan said there was no reserve water that could replace Hagbyån.

nybroasen_teoretiskt_max_uttag.name: Theoretical maximum abstraction from the Nybroåsen esker (Nybro and Kalmar)
nybroasen_teoretiskt_max_uttag.note: A rough estimate of the theoretical maximum, not a permit. The same table gives 1.2 million m³/year for Hagbyån with lake Hultebräan (Kalmar's infiltration source) and 1.8 million m³/year for Ljungbyån with lake Orranäsasjön. For comparison, Kalmar produced 5.4 million m³ of drinking water in 2025, about half from infiltrated river water, and Nybro also draws on the esker.

hagbymassivet_naturlig_grundvattenbildni.name: Natural groundwater recharge in Hagbymassivet, Kalmar's main wellfield area in Nybroåsen
hagbymassivet_naturlig_grundvattenbildni.note: SGU gives 40–45 l/s, i.e. 1.3–1.4 million m³/year, while abstraction in the area was about 140 l/s (4.4 million m³/year) thanks to basin infiltration since the late 1950s. SGU judged that abstraction could rise to 300 l/s with more infiltration, and named the Fröstorp and Råsbäck areas (each at least about 25 l/s) as the most important future additions. Kalmar Vatten is now seeking a new water permit for Hockland and Fröstorp.

reservvattentakter_kapacitet_kalmar.name: Combined capacity of Kalmar's reserve water sources
reservvattentakter_kapacitet_kalmar.note: Sum of the stated capacities of nine small reserve wells (Halltorp 1 and 2, Tvärskog, Påryd/Ugglebo, Trekanten, Norra Hagby, Lindsdal, Läckeby, Rockneby): 43 l/s, own calculation. That is about 25 % of mean production in 2025; the 2013 regional plan gave about 3,400 m³/day. They are small groundwater sources that are also hit by drought, and in 2020 it was unclear whether they would be kept.

dricksvatten_sasongsokning_juli_kalmar.name: Increase in Kalmar's drinking water production in July compared with January
dricksvatten_sasongsokning_juli_kalmar.note: Production in July was about 3,900 m³/day higher than in January 2010, roughly 25 % of the annual mean of 15,600 m³/day (5.7 million m³, own calculation). No newer figure for peak day or installed capacity was found. In Borgholm, July abstraction was 2.4 times January's in the same year.

kalmar_vatten_investeringar_2026_2032.name: Kalmar Vatten's planned investments over seven years (2026–2032)
kalmar_vatten_investeringar_2026_2032.note: Of which 834 million SEK in 2026; the plan is dominated by the Kalmarsundsverket treatment plant and pipe renewal. The drinking-water projects are a rebuild of the Yxneberga infiltration plant for more capacity, a new raw-water main from Bottorp to Kalmar (2027), an extra pumping line at Skälby, a new water permit for Hockland and Fröstorp (about 5 years) and backup power, with a study of running fully for three months without grid power. The water operations themselves invested 46 million SEK in 2025.

torsas_dricksvatten_fran_kalmar_andel.name: Share of Torsås municipality's public drinking water bought from Kalmar
torsas_dricksvatten_fran_kalmar_andel.note: Kalmar Vatten has supplied Torsås since 2001 (about 0.37 million m³/year according to the 2013 plan) and, since 2016, Öland by pipeline as well. Sales to Torsås were 1.8 million SEK and to the two Öland municipalities 0.35 million SEK in 2025 (annual report). Kalmar is thus the hub and supplier in regional cooperation, not a recipient.

kalmarsundsverket_atervunnet_vatten_kapa.name: Capacity for recycled water from the Kalmarsundsverket plant (from 2027)
kalmarsundsverket_atervunnet_vatten_kapa.note: Planned capacity at class A quality under EU Regulation 2020/741, 50–80 % of incoming wastewater (5.2 million m³ in 2025); this equals about 80 % of today's mean drinking-water production. The first planned uses are a water kiosk, the plant's own process water (about 200 m³/day) and possibly toilet flushing etc. at the county hospital (250–300 m³/day, about 10 million SEK according to Region Kalmar's pre-study). Drinking water from recycled water is being studied through a two-year pilot that needs external funding.

tekniskt_vatten_bevattningsbehov_kalmar.name: Estimated demand for technical (recycled) water for irrigation in Kalmar
tekniskt_vatten_bevattningsbehov_kalmar.note: Midpoint of 113,000–172,500 m³/year for users such as Kalmar golf club, football pitches, parks and allotments. That is 2–3 % of annual production but falls on the summer peak; football pitches (about 34,000 m³/year) are watered mostly with drinking water today. A separate pipe network is judged too costly, so water kiosks and point solutions are more realistic.

atervunnet_vatten_pilot_kostnad_kalmar.name: Production cost of recycled water in the municipal irrigation pilot
atervunnet_vatten_pilot_kostnad_kalmar.note: A UV unit for treated wastewater (investment 1.69 million SEK plus about 0.2 million SEK, 10-year depreciation, 4 % interest) at today's use of about 1,500 m³ a year, although capacity is 864 m³/day. After EU and HaV grants (90 %), the municipality's cost is about 15 SEK/m³, against about 34 SEK/m³ for drinking water. The cost per m³ falls steeply with larger volumes.

avsaltning_sandvik_kapacitet.name: Capacity of the Sandvik desalination plant, Borgholm municipality (Öland)
avsaltning_sandvik_kapacitet.note: Brackish water is drawn from 28 m depth in Kalmarsund and desalinated by reverse osmosis; the plant was built in record time (ground broken August 2016, opened June 2017) and supplies about 3,000 households. According to SVT (2017) it cost 85 million SEK plus 28 million SEK for pipelines, and it takes in 6,000 m³ of seawater a day. Energy use is not published.

avsaltning_morbylanga_kapacitet.name: Capacity of the Mörbylånga desalination and reuse waterworks (Öland)
avsaltning_morbylanga_kapacitet.note: The plant (opened 2019) treats brackish groundwater from beach wells (up to 5,800 m³/day of raw water) and up to 1,500 m³/day of process water from the Guldfågeln food plant's treatment works; losses in the plant are just over 30 %. The municipality describes it as the first in Sweden to reuse used water as drinking water. Together with Sandvik, Öland has 7,000 m³/day, about 2.5 million m³/year, that does not depend on rain.

avsaltning_morbylanga_investering.name: Investment in the Mörbylånga desalination and reuse waterworks (Öland)
avsaltning_morbylanga_investering.note: The municipality's forecast in spring 2019 was about 110 million SEK, and its water services plan gives about 180 million SEK for the two waterworks built since 2015. Per m³/day of capacity that is about 33,000 SEK, close to Sandvik (85 million SEK for 3,000 m³/day, about 28,000 SEK; own calculation).

morbylanga_forbrukning_hogsasong.name: Drinking water use in Mörbylånga municipality in high season (Öland)
morbylanga_forbrukning_hogsasong.note: Against about 3,500 m³/day in low season, i.e. 57 % higher in summer. The municipality delivered about 1.4 million m³ in 2023 to almost 70 % of its 15,700 residents and expects use to exceed 2 million m³ a year by 2037 if growth continues (water services plan 2025–2037). The 4,000 m³/day desalination plant thus covers just under three quarters of summer demand.

borgholm_vattenuttag_juli_jamfort_januar.name: Water abstraction in Borgholm municipality in July compared with January (Öland)
borgholm_vattenuttag_juli_jamfort_januar.note: Several waterworks then reach maximum capacity. In 2010 abstraction was 3,890 m³/day in January and 9,208 in July (2.4 times, 2013 regional plan), and SVT reported about 110,000 m³ in January and 260,000 m³ in July 2024. The municipality's six waterworks produce about 2 million m³ a year, and about 70 % of 11,000 residents are connected.

befolkning_borgholm_juli_okning.name: Increase in people present in Borgholm municipality in July compared with October–November (Öland)
befolkning_borgholm_juli_okning.note: From about 10,900 to 52,200 people, according to SCB's experimental statistics from mobile network data. Mörbylånga rose 73 % (16,000 to 27,600), Öland as a whole roughly tripled, while Kalmar municipality rose 1 %. In summer 2023 Borgholm's peak population was 4.5 times its annual median.

ledning_fastland_oland_kapacitet.name: Capacity of the drinking water pipeline across Kalmarsund (Öland)
ledning_fastland_oland_kapacitet.note: The pipeline across Kalmarsund was built during the 2016 water crisis and still carries water from Kalmar Vatten. Mörbylånga gives about 7.3 million SEK for the pipeline with a booster station, which can carry water both ways and on to Borgholm. Its capacity is about 7 % of Kalmar's mean production and about a fifth of Mörbylånga's summer demand.

vattentransporter_morbylanga_2016_kostna.name: Cost of water transports to Mörbylånga during the 2016 water crisis (Öland)
vattentransporter_morbylanga_2016_kostna.note: When drinking water ran out in Mörbylånga in 2016, tankers carried 1,000 m³ a day from the mainland through spring, summer and autumn. The waterworks that desalinates and treats sea and industrial water was then built for 130 million SEK. According to the regional plan, groundwater on northern Öland reached a record low in November 2016.

bevattningsforbud_borgholm_dagar.name: Days per year with a garden-watering ban on municipal water in Borgholm municipality (Öland)
bevattningsforbud_borgholm_dagar.note: The ban recurs every year, both because rainfall is low and because the summer load can cause supply problems and poorer water quality. Pools of 3 m³ or more may not be filled from the mains. Kalmar, by contrast, has had no restrictions since summer 2016.

grundvatten_god_status_morbylanga.name: Groundwater bodies with good chemical and quantitative status in Mörbylånga municipality (Öland)
grundvatten_god_status_morbylanga.note: Borgholm has 22.2 %, Kalmar municipality 77.8 %, the county 90 % and Sweden 97 % (Kolada 2022). Mörbylånga's water services plan states that all groundwater bodies on Öland have poor quantitative but good chemical status.

grundvattentorrar_nybroasen_andel_2016_2.name: Share of years 2016–2026 with groundwater drought in the natural parts of Nybroåsen
grundvattentorrar_nybroasen_andel_2016_2.note: Own analysis: a drought year has at least three months below the 10th percentile of the same month in 1961–1990. Both stations give 2016, 2025 and 2026 (data to 9 September), against 6 of 29 years in 1961–1990 and 1 of 25 in 1991–2015; in winter 2025/26 station 6_26 was only 0.1 m above its 1964 record. Station 6_23, in the infiltrated area, had no drought year in 2016–2026.

grundvattentorrar_oland_andel_2016_2026.name: Share of years 2016–2026 with groundwater drought at SGU's Böda station, northern Öland (Öland)
grundvattentorrar_oland_andel_2016_2026.note: Own analysis with the same definition as for Nybroåsen: drought years 2016, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2025 and 2026, against 3 of 23 years in 1968–1990. The neighbouring station Böda_9 gives 6 of 11 years, and both had their lowest levels since 1968 in October 2016. The series has over 23,000 values and must be fetched in several pages (startIndex); abstraction at nearby wellfields may affect the levels.

grundvattenbildning_nybroasen_2071_2100_.name: Change in groundwater recharge at Kalmar's wellfields in Nybroåsen, 2071–2100 (RCP8.5 ≈ SSP5-8.5)
grundvattenbildning_nybroasen_2071_2100_.note: Mean of 17 simulations against 1971–2000 (149 mm/year); the range is ±1 standard deviation, and 15 of 17 simulations show a decrease. RCP4.5 ≈ SSP2-4.5 gives −7.1 % in 2041–2070 and −4.6 % in 2071–2100, and RCP8.5 gives −9.6 % in 2041–2070. Spring recharge falls most (−29 % in 2071–2100 under RCP8.5).

grundvattenbildning_torrar_nybroasen_207.name: Change in groundwater recharge in a dry year at Kalmar's wellfields in Nybroåsen, 2071–2100 (RCP8.5 ≈ SSP5-8.5)
grundvattenbildning_torrar_nybroasen_207.note: A dry year is the 25th percentile of annual values, so dry years worsen more than the average year (−22.6 %). Under RCP4.5 ≈ SSP2-4.5 the change is −8.1 % in 2041–2070 and −10.2 % in 2071–2100, and under RCP8.5 −19.9 % in 2041–2070. The range is ±1 standard deviation across 17 simulations.

langsta_grundvattentorka_okning_nybroase.name: Lengthening of the year's longest groundwater drought at Kalmar's wellfields in Nybroåsen, 2071–2100 (RCP8.5 ≈ SSP5-8.5)
langsta_grundvattentorka_okning_nybroase.note: A groundwater drought is a period when recharge over the last 30 days is below 10 mm; the longest such period was about 187 days in 1971–2000, and all 17 simulations show it getting longer. RCP4.5 ≈ SSP2-4.5 gives +15.8 days in 2041–2070 and +14.9 days in 2071–2100, and RCP8.5 gives +22.0 days in 2041–2070. A dry year lengthens by 37 days under RCP8.5.

grundvattenbildning_oland_2071_2100_ssp5.name: Change in groundwater recharge at Borgholm's main wellfield, 2071–2100 (Öland, RCP8.5 ≈ SSP5-8.5)
grundvattenbildning_oland_2071_2100_ssp5.note: The area is at Solbergafältet, Borgholm's largest wellfield; the 1971–2000 reference is 144 mm/year. Böda on northern Öland gets −34 % and Mörbylånga −22 %, and a dry year falls by 41 % at Köpingsvik and 54 % at Böda. Under RCP4.5 ≈ SSP2-4.5 the change at Köpingsvik is −11.5 % in 2041–2070 and −7.3 % in 2071–2100.

lagvattenforing_hagbyan_2071_2100_rcp85.name: Change in mean low flow (MLQ) in the river Hagbyån, the source of Kalmar's artificial infiltration, 2071–2100 (RCP8.5 ≈ SSP5-8.5)
lagvattenforing_hagbyan_2071_2100_rcp85.note: All 17 models show a decrease; the range is min–max. RCP4.5 ≈ SSP2-4.5 gives −9.9 % in 2041–2070 and −6.7 % in 2071–2100, and RCP8.5 gives −11.1 % in 2041–2070. Kalmar Vatten tops up the river in summer from its lake reservoir, so lower low flows mean the reservoir empties faster.

torrar_sannolikhet_nybroasen_2071_2100_s.name: Annual probability of a recharge year as dry as today's 1-in-10 dry year at Kalmar's wellfields, 2071–2100 (RCP8.5 ≈ SSP5-8.5)
torrar_sannolikhet_nybroasen_2071_2100_s.note: Own estimate: annual values are assumed normally distributed with the mean and 25th percentile from SGU, and the threshold is today's 1-in-10 dry year (10 % a year in 1971–2000). RCP4.5 ≈ SSP2-4.5 gives 9 % in 2041–2070 and 11 % in 2071–2100, and RCP8.5 ≈ SSP5-8.5 gives 15 % in 2041–2070 and 21 % in 2071–2100, i.e. about one year in five. For Böda on northern Öland it is 16–18 % (SSP2-4.5) and 19–24 % (SSP5-8.5).

gastnatter_kalmar_kommun.name: Guest nights in commercial accommodation in Kalmar Municipality
gastnatter_kalmar_kommun.note: Hotels, holiday villages, hostels, campsites and commercially mediated private cottages and flats (SoL). Multiplying Kolada N45850 (guest nights per inhabitant) by population gives 418,023 (2019), 343,499 (2020), 428,410 (2023) and 445,963 (2024): +8% since 2019, and 6.2 guest nights per inhabitant in 2025 (Sweden 6.7). Kolada's 2022 value (44.4 per inhabitant) is clearly wrong and was not used.

gastnatter_kalmar_lan.name: Guest nights in commercial accommodation in Kalmar County
gastnatter_kalmar_lan.note: Fifth highest of Sweden's counties; −1.0% on 2024 (3,340,127) but +17% on 2019 (2,822,492 from Kolada N45850 times population). Accommodation revenue was SEK 1,189 million, and there were 13 guest nights per inhabitant (Sweden about 7). Region Kalmar län's report gives a rounded 3.4 million and +1.8%, which differs from Tillväxtverket's final figures.

gastnatter_borgholm.name: Guest nights in commercial accommodation in Borgholm Municipality (Öland)
gastnatter_borgholm.note: The county's largest tourism municipality, with 102 guest nights per inhabitant (10,626 inhabitants). Kolada N45850 times population gives 1,016,297 (2019) and 1,115,271 (2024), so 2025 was −3.2%. Together with Mörbylånga, Öland had 1,443,657 guest nights in 2025, 44% of the county's total.

gastnatter_morbylanga.name: Guest nights in commercial accommodation in Mörbylånga Municipality (Öland)
gastnatter_morbylanga.note: 22 guest nights per inhabitant (16,306 inhabitants). Kolada N45850 times population gives 369,521 (2019) and 362,536 (2024), so the level is broadly unchanged since 2019.

gastnatter_utlandsk_andel_lan.name: Foreign guests' share of guest nights in Kalmar County
gastnatter_utlandsk_andel_lan.note: Swedish guests accounted for 80.2% in 2025. Foreign guest nights were about 640,000, about 15,000 fewer than in 2024; Germany is the largest market and the USA grew fastest (+19%). Tillväxtverket's Figure 1.8 gives 20% (Sweden 26%), and for 2024 the figure is 19.7% (Visita) or 21% (Region Kalmar län), depending on how guests with unknown home country are counted.

gastnatter_sommarandel_lan.name: Share of the county's guest nights falling in June–August
gastnatter_sommarandel_lan.note: "About 72 per cent" in 2025, against 75% in 2024 and 73% in 2023; nationally the share is 43% (Tillväxtverket). The season is widening: April 2025 had about 50,000 more guest nights than April 2024 (+60%), May about 40,000 more (+16%) and September about 35,000 more (+23%). The county's visitor-economy strategy aims to make it a year-round destination by 2030.

gastnatter_camping_andel_lan.name: Campsites' share of guest nights in Kalmar County
gastnatter_camping_andel_lan.note: The highest camping share of any county (Halland 53%, whereas hotels account for 91% in Stockholm County). Camping grew by about 20,000 guest nights in 2025 and earns about 32% of the county's accommodation revenue; hotels earn just over half (Region Kalmar län). Camping-heavy tourism is especially sensitive to weather, beaches and water quality.

korttidsuthyrning_gastnatter_lan.name: Guest nights booked through short-term rental platforms in Kalmar County
korttidsuthyrning_gastnatter_lan.note: The series is 115,604 (2018), 164,752 (2019), 124,668 (2020), 188,916 (2021), 256,094 (2022), 322,537 (2023) and 425,481 (2024): +268% since 2018. That adds about 13% on top of the county's commercial guest nights in 2024 (own calculation). The statistics are experimental and may partly overlap the SoL category in the accommodation statistics.

belaggningsgrad_kalmar_kommun.name: Occupancy rate in commercial accommodation in Kalmar Municipality
belaggningsgrad_kalmar_kommun.note: The highest in the county in 2025, ahead of Oskarshamn (54%); Borgholm had 42% and Mörbylånga 39.1%. High occupancy points to steadier demand through the year (conferences and business travel). Kalmar's destination strategy (2024) names a shortage of hotel, conference and arena capacity as a weakness.

logiintakter_kalmar_kommun.name: Accommodation revenue in commercial accommodation in Kalmar Municipality
logiintakter_kalmar_kommun.note: SEK 263,980,018 in 2025 (SEK 262,911,689 in 2024). Borgholm had SEK 278.9 million and Mörbylånga SEK 114.1 million; the county SEK 1,188.6 million (Tillväxtverket). Per guest night this is about SEK 584 in Kalmar but about SEK 258 in Borgholm (own calculation), reflecting hotels in the city and camping on Öland.

turismkonsumtion_kalmar_kommun.name: Tourism consumption in Kalmar Municipality (inbound visitors)
turismkonsumtion_kalmar_kommun.note: Spending in the municipality by visitors from elsewhere, from Tillväxtverket's regional tourism accounts: SEK 2,539 million in 2024 and SEK 2,748 million in 2025, or SEK 37,609 per inhabitant. Borgholm had SEK 2,463 million (SEK 231,790 per inhabitant) and Mörbylånga SEK 1,105 million. In Kalmar, retail is the largest product group; on Öland, accommodation is.

turismkonsumtion_kalmar_lan.name: Tourism consumption in Kalmar County (inbound visitors)
turismkonsumtion_kalmar_lan.note: "About 11 billion" in 2025; the municipal values sum to SEK 11,102 million (SEK 10,600 million in 2024). Retail accounts for 32%, accommodation 30%, second homes/flats 14% and culture 3%. Inbound domestic tourism exceeded county residents' own tourism elsewhere in Sweden by about SEK 1.6 billion.

turism_foradlingsvarde_andel_kalmar_komm.name: Tourism's share of value added in Kalmar Municipality
turism_foradlingsvarde_andel_kalmar_komm.note: Own calculation: tourism value added of SEK 607 million divided by the municipality's total value added of SEK 29,340 million (current prices, 2022). For the whole county the share is 2.3% (2,118 of 92,273 SEK million). Tourism value added in Kalmar was SEK 609 million in 2023.

turism_foradlingsvarde_andel_borgholm.name: Tourism's share of value added in Borgholm Municipality (Öland)
turism_foradlingsvarde_andel_borgholm.note: Own calculation: SEK 334 million of the municipality's SEK 2,935 million (current prices, 2022), five times Kalmar's share. Mörbylånga is at 4.5% (178 of 3,997 SEK million). Borgholm's tourism value added rose to SEK 442 million in 2023.

turism_arsarbetskrafter_kalmar_kommun.name: Full-time equivalents in tourism production in Kalmar Municipality
turism_arsarbetskrafter_kalmar_kommun.note: 1,004.87 FTEs in 2022 according to the tourism accounts; Borgholm 275, Mörbylånga 193 and the county 2,676 in total (own sum). This corresponds to about 2.6% of the 39,331 people employed at workplaces in the municipality in 2024, although FTEs and persons are different measures.

besoksnaring_anstallda_lan.name: Employees in accommodation and restaurants in Kalmar County
besoksnaring_anstallda_lan.note: 694 units (88 accommodation, 606 restaurants) with 4,584 employees and SEK 3,893 million in domestic turnover excluding VAT in 2024. The visitor economy generated SEK 885 million in tax revenue in 2023 (SEK 294 million in employer contributions and SEK 591 million in VAT). The industry expects to need 1,661 hires over the next three years.

sommarbefolkning_borgholm_juli.name: People present in Borgholm Municipality at night in July (Öland)
sommarbefolkning_borgholm_juli.note: Mobile network data at 03:00–05:00: 10,880 people in October–November, 42,940 at Midsummer and 52,160 in July 2022, i.e. +379%. Mörbylånga rose from 15,970 to 27,610 (+73%), while Kalmar was unchanged (+0.8% in July, −4.8% at Midsummer). The figure of 250,000 people in Borgholm in summer quoted in the media could not be substantiated.

oland_befolkning_juli_faktor.name: Öland's population in July relative to October–November (Öland)
oland_befolkning_juli_faktor.note: Own calculation from SCB's table: (52,160 + 27,610) / (10,880 + 15,970) = 79,770 / 26,850. That is about 52,900 more people on the island on July nights in 2022. The value is a monthly average; individual peak days are higher.

fritidshus_per_1000_borgholm.name: Second homes per 1,000 inhabitants in Borgholm Municipality (Öland)
fritidshus_per_1000_borgholm.note: About 9,200 second homes (own conversion using population). Mörbylånga has 255 per 1,000 (about 4,150), Kalmar 31 (about 2,300) and Sweden 60, so Öland has about 13,300 second homes. According to Region Kalmar län, about 10% of the county's second homes have foreign owners; 2,268 are German-owned, the most in Sweden.

vatten_borgholm_juli.name: Water consumption in Borgholm Municipality in July (Öland)
vatten_borgholm_juli.note: About 260,000 m³ in July against about 110,000 m³ in January, i.e. 2.4 times as much. Combined with SCB's mobile data, the extra use is about 120 litres per additional person per day (own calculation: 150,000 m³ over 31 days divided by 41,280 additional people). Borgholm Energi produces about 1.8 million m³ of drinking water a year and runs a desalination plant.

bilandel_turistresor_lan.name: Car share of domestic tourist trips to Kalmar County
bilandel_turistresor_lan.note: The report states that the car share is highest in Jönköping, Kalmar and Dalarna counties (91–92%) and lowest in Stockholm (43%), using data for 2017–2021; 91.5 is the midpoint. The car's share of domestic tourist trips nationally rose by 14 percentage points during the pandemic years. The Öland Bridge is the island's only fixed link.

kalmar_lans_museum_besok.name: Visits to Kalmar läns museum (county museum)
kalmar_lans_museum_besok.note: 86,978 visits in 2024 (+5.7%). Kalmar konstmuseum had 26,650 visits in 2025 (22,144 in 2024, including Designarkivet in Nybro) and Ölands museum Himmelsberga 29,171. Kalmar Castle has about 190,000 visitors a year (see kalmar_slott_besokare).

ironman_kalmar_omsattning.name: Tourism turnover generated by Ironman Kalmar
ironman_kalmar_omsattning.note: Destination Kalmar's estimate using the Event Impact Calculator tool. More than 3,000 triathletes have registered for the 2027 race (sold out in one hour); each athlete stays four nights on average with four companions, and in 2025 half of the 2,850 participants came from abroad. That is roughly 60,000 person-nights in one week of August (own rough calculation).

skordefest_besokare_oland.name: Visitors to Öland's Harvest Festival (Skördefest) (Öland)
skordefest_besokare_oland.note: Expected visitors in 2018, with over 900 activities across the island. The festival is held on the last weekend of September and thus extends the season. No later official figure was found.

kryssningsanlop_kalmar.name: Cruise ship calls in Kalmar
kryssningsanlop_kalmar.note: Two calls (Ocean Nova and Ocean Majesty) with about 700 guests were expected in 2019, against one call in 2018. Cruise tourism is thus negligible compared with 452,000 commercial guest nights. Kalmar Hamn publishes no cruise statistics.

badvatten_eu_utmarkt_antal.name: EU bathing waters of excellent quality (Kalmar Municipality and Öland)
badvatten_eu_utmarkt_antal.note: 2025 classification under the Bathing Water Directive (E. coli and enterococci over four seasons): Kalmar's 4 and Mörbylånga's 6 are excellent, while Borgholm has 13 excellent, 2 good and 2 sufficient (Böda Riviera/Kyrketorp and Byrum-Sandvik). Böda Riviera was classed as poor in 2024. Algal blooms are not part of the classification.

badplatser_cyanorisk_oland_antal.name: Bathing sites on Öland with cyanobacterial bloom risk in their bathing water profile (Öland)
badplatser_cyanorisk_oland_antal.note: Borgholm 10 of 17 and Mörbylånga 12 of 14 sites have bloom risk flagged; none of Kalmar Municipality's 26 sites has. The official 2026 bathing season was only 21 June–15 August.

badvattenprover_algblomning_antal.name: Bathing water samples with an observed algal bloom (Kalmar Municipality and Öland)
badvattenprover_algblomning_antal.note: Own count in the sample results (/{id}/results) for 57 bathing sites: 1, 1, 2, 4 and 3 samples with a bloom in 2022–2026, 10 of the 11 on Öland. Samples are taken only 3–4 times a season and only until mid-August, so short blooms are poorly captured. 9 samples were unfit for bathing because of bacteria.

oland_algblomning_turismforlust_2005.name: Tourism losses in the 2005 algal bloom summer (Öland)
oland_algblomning_turismforlust_2005.note: The authors report losses of 17–23 million euros for Öland's tourism industry in summer 2005; the abstract does not describe the method. The following summer, with daily algae monitoring ("Miss Algae"), this turned into a gain of 17 million euros. The value 20 is the midpoint.

jrc_turismefterfragan_se21_sommar.name: Increase in summer and early-autumn tourism demand in Småland with the islands at 3–4 °C global warming
jrc_turismefterfragan_se21_sommar.note: Panel model of 269 EU regions, 2000–2019: a 1% better climate comfort (Tourism Climate Index) gives 0.57% more bed nights, 1.2% in coastal regions. The coastal region SE21 (which includes Kalmar County) is projected to gain more than +5% demand in summer and early autumn at 3–4 °C, while the EU as a whole gains 1.58% at 4 °C and July falls by 5.7% across Europe.

varldsarv_betesmark_havsniva_25m.name: Grazed alvar and shore meadows in the World Heritage site affected by a 2.5 m sea-level rise (Öland)
varldsarv_betesmark_havsniva_25m.note: GIS analysis: 900 ha are affected at +1 m and 3,000 ha at +2.5 m, and 13,000 ha lie in areas that can flood during heavy high flows. Of the site's 18 harbours and boathouse sites, 7 are affected at +1 m and all at +2.5 m. The World Heritage site covers just over 56,000 ha (Swedish National Heritage Board) and depends on continued grazing and farming.

invanare_turism_trafikproblem_andel.name: Residents who think tourism increases traffic problems in their municipality
invanare_turism_trafikproblem_andel.note: Survey of county residents with 1,864 responses (response rate 23%). At the same time, 85% agreed that tourism improves the local economy and 80% were positive about tourism development, while 40% thought more tourism harms natural areas and 9% that tourists affect their daily life negatively.

utslapp_per_gastnatt.name: Climate impact per tourist guest night (West Sweden)
utslapp_per_gastnatt.note: Life-cycle calculation for tourism in West Sweden: 110 kg CO2e per tourist and 39 kg per guest night, of which travel to and from the destination is 54% and accommodation 23%. Applying the same factor, Kalmar Municipality's 452,248 guest nights give about 17,600 tonnes a year and Öland's about 56,000 tonnes (own rough calculation). With 91–92% of trips by car, the transport share in Kalmar County is probably at least as large.

lnu_helarsstudenter_totalt.name: Full-time equivalent students at Linnaeus University as a whole (Kalmar and Växjö)
lnu_helarsstudenter_totalt.note: Covers the whole university including distance learning (39% of full-time equivalents in 2025, 41% in 2024); the schema has no level for Kalmar + Kronoberg, hence Kalmar County. The series is 16,383 (2020), 16,180 (2021), 15,640 (2022), 15,642 (2023), 15,128 (2024) and 15,440 (2025), i.e. −5.8% since 2020. The funding ceiling for education is being lowered for 2025–2027, and in 2025 the university delivered 104% of its ceiling according to the Swedish Higher Education Authority (UKÄ), i.e. teaching beyond what the state pays for.

lnu_andel_verksamhet_kalmar.name: Kalmar's share of Linnaeus University's activity
lnu_andel_verksamhet_kalmar.note: Own estimate from three independent measures: 16,000 of 44,000 registered students belong to Kalmar according to lnu.se (36%), about 6,000 of 16,180 full-time equivalents in 2021 according to Kalmar Municipality (37%), and Universitetskajen's 48,800 of the university's 131,300 leased m² in 2023 (37%); in 2015 the university itself gave about 40% (Barometern). Region Kalmar County's minutes of 2024-03-20 state about 8,000 full-time equivalents in Kalmar (≈ 51%), which does not match the other sources and probably counts differently.

registrerade_studenter_kalmar.name: Registered students belonging to the Kalmar campus
registrerade_studenter_kalmar.note: Linnaeus University's website states that about 16,000 of 44,000 students belong to Kalmar and 28,000 to Växjö; the figure is undated, but the total of 44,000 matches the situation around 2021–2022. In 2025 the whole university had 40,259 registered students, and at the same share (36%) Kalmar would have about 14,500 (own calculation). The figure counts heads including distance students, not people living in Kalmar.

campusstudenter_kalmar_uppskattning.name: Full-time equivalent students studying on site in Kalmar (estimate)
campusstudenter_kalmar_uppskattning.note: Own estimate: the municipality's figure of about 6,000 full-time equivalents in Kalmar includes distance study, which made up 39% of the university's full-time equivalents in 2025 (61% × 6,000 ≈ 3,700). Kalmar's own distance share is unknown, hence the range of 25–50% distance; on top of this come about 120 medical students from Linköping University.

lnu_anstallda_kalmar_uppskattning.name: Linnaeus University employees in Kalmar (estimate)
lnu_anstallda_kalmar_uppskattning.note: Own estimate: 36–40% of the university's 2,145 employees (2025 average) gives 770–860; the university publishes no breakdown by campus. Already in 2019 about 400 staff worked in the Magna, Radix and Vita buildings, before the School of Business and Economics, the library and the administration had moved in. This is about 2% of the 39,331 jobs in the municipality.

lnu_doktorander_totalt.name: Active doctoral students at Linnaeus University as a whole
lnu_doktorander_totalt.note: Down from 315 (2021) and 306 (2024), and new admissions fell to 34 in 2025 from 55 in 2023. 155 full-time equivalents were employed as doctoral students and 51 doctoral degrees were awarded in 2025. No split between Kalmar and Växjö is published.

lakarstudenter_kalmar.name: Medical students in Kalmar (Linköping University's medical programme)
lakarstudenter_kalmar.note: Since 2019, medical students from Linköping can take the clinical part (six semesters) in Kalmar, about 20 places per semester based at the county hospital; Linnaeus University and Region Kalmar County take part. In 2021 there were 117 medical students in Kalmar, and of the first 14 who graduated that year, 9 stayed to work for Region Kalmar County (Kalmar Municipality 2022).

sjofartshogskolan_studenter.name: Programme students at Kalmar Maritime Academy
sjofartshogskolan_studenter.note: Kalmar Maritime Academy was founded in 1842 and trains master mariners, marine engineers and operating technicians; almost as many again take single courses and contract education. About 10% of the students are women, and since 2010 the university has graduated 925 master mariners and marine engineers (vice-chancellor, 2024), about 60 a year. Training relies on simulators, and research covers working life and risk, the environmental impact of shipping and marine spatial planning, and energy efficiency.

universitetskajen_forhyrd_yta.name: Floor area leased by Linnaeus University at Universitetskajen
universitetskajen_forhyrd_yta.note: Sum of two rows in the premises plan (Intea/Eldaren 6: 27,000 m², P&E/Eldaren 1: 21,800 m²), 37% of the university's 131,300 m²; Växjö (Vöfab) has 78,400 m². Six connected buildings in Ölandshamnen next to Kalmar Central Station house all faculties, the library and the administration; the campus was completed in 2020 and inaugurated on 27 August 2021 (ground broken in January 2016). The university judges its Kalmar premises to have low utilisation at high cost, with 2% of the area vacant against 0.5% in Växjö.

universitetskajen_forsta_hyresavtal_lope.name: Year in which the first lease at Universitetskajen expires
universitetskajen_forsta_hyresavtal_lope.note: The eastern part (the Vita, Culmen and Stella buildings, with health and life sciences, the university library, the main lecture hall and the administration) is rented from Intea on two ten-year leases that expire in 2028 and 2030; the western part (Forma, Magna and Radix) has a 20-year lease with Kalmar Eldaren AB (P&E) until 2038. The expiries are natural decision points for where activities should be located, at the same time as the university must save about SEK 120 million in 2027–2029.

tidigare_universitetsadresser_kalmar.name: Addresses across which Linnaeus University in Kalmar was spread before Universitetskajen
tidigare_universitetsadresser_kalmar.note: Plans for a single, city-integrated university began around 2008 and the move took place in 2018–2021, reducing the university's total leased area. Akademiska Hus, which owned about 28,000 m² in Kalmar, sold just over 16,000 m² in 2012 (nine buildings on southern Malmen and Rostad, including the then library) to LW Fastigheter, and in 2013 the harbour property that became the western part of Universitetskajen. What the older buildings are used for today could not be verified.

lmo_provtagningstillfallen.name: Sampling occasions at the Linnaeus Microbial Observatory (LMO) in the Baltic Sea since 2011
lmo_provtagningstillfallen.note: A time series 11 km off Kårehamn on Öland's east coast, sampled about every second week since 2011 (status May 2026); the samples are analysed in the laboratory in Kalmar by up to ten people. It is complemented by the Kalmar Strait Station (K-station) opposite Kalmar Castle, sampled weekly since March 2018; both are part of the government-funded research programme EcoChange.

eemis_medarbetare.name: Staff of the EEMiS centre of excellence (ecology and evolution in aquatic systems)
eemis_medarbetare.note: EEMiS studies Baltic Sea food webs from microbes to fish and birds; the figure includes students, doctoral students, technicians, postdocs and principal investigators. The centre runs LMO, the K-station, a warming bay and acoustic monitoring, and the Linnaeus Knowledge Environment Water is part of it. In 2024 the EEMiS microbiologist Jarone Pinhassi became the university's first Wallenberg Scholar, with an unrestricted grant of SEK 20 million over five years (annual report 2024).

ecodriving_bransle_besparing.name: Fuel saving from simulator-based eco-driving training (Kalmar Maritime Academy)
ecodriving_bransle_besparing.note: Courses for masters of small passenger ferries in the Stockholm archipelago have cut fuel use by up to 13%. Since 2015 more than 400 crew members on the Swedish Transport Administration's road ferries have been trained (1.5 litres less per crossing, a claimed 11,000 tonnes of CO₂ a year), and more than 700 officers in total. The figures are the simulator maker Kongsberg's account of a Linnaeus University report that has not been reviewed here.

lnu_forskningsintakter.name: Revenue for research and doctoral education, Linnaeus University as a whole
lnu_forskningsintakter.note: This is 31% of total revenue of SEK 2,435 million (own calculation), and 45% of research revenue is external. The goals for 2026–2030 say research should become as large a part of the university as education, and that external funding should make up 50% of research funding. The split between Kalmar and Växjö is not reported.

ehalsa_magister_sokande.name: Applicants to the master's programme in eHealth (eHealth collaboration with Region Kalmar County)
ehalsa_magister_sokande.note: The eHealth collaboration is a joint ten-year initiative (2022–2032) of Linnaeus University and Region Kalmar County covering education, research, infrastructure and innovation. In 2025 a graduate school with seven doctoral students in health and data science started, and a professor of health informatics took up the post on 1 January 2026; the programme is described as unique in Sweden.

rattsvetenskap_satsning_mnkr.name: Legal science initiative in Kalmar (Kalmar Municipality and Linnaeus University)
rattsvetenskap_satsning_mnkr.unit: SEK million over ten years (at least)
rattsvetenskap_satsning_mnkr.note: Under the agreement of December 2021 the municipality contributes SEK 100 million and the university at least SEK 200 million, aiming for a law degree programme with first admission no later than 2027. The bachelor's programme in legal science started in 2024 (60 students) and had 587 applicants for 70 places in 2025; the unit gained degree-awarding powers at master's and doctoral level in 2025, and the application to award the professional law degree (juristexamen) was submitted in September 2025 (annual report 2025).

kommunens_forskningsavtal_mnkr_per_ar.name: Kalmar Municipality's annual grant to Linnaeus University for research, development and growth
kommunens_forskningsavtal_mnkr_per_ar.unit: SEK million per year (for ten years)
kommunens_forskningsavtal_mnkr_per_ar.note: Agreement signed on 2 February 2018 for SEK 1.5 million a year for ten years to strengthen the university in Kalmar, cooperation with business and growth. In 2019 the municipal group reported a record SEK 2.7 million in research funding. The strategic partnership with Växjö Municipality and the Linnaeus students' union (since 2017, now 2026–2028) has no budget of its own.

kvarstannande_examinerade_3ar.name: Linnaeus University graduates still living in Kalmar or Kronoberg County three years after graduating
kvarstannande_examinerade_3ar.note: The 'stayers' measure for the 8,800 who graduated in 2015–2017; just under two thirds moved away from the region. Of those recruited locally (from Kalmar and Kronoberg counties) 78.6% still lived there, but only 16.6% of those recruited from the rest of the country. Covers both counties, not Kalmar Municipality alone.

examinerade_bor_i_kalmar_lan_2017.name: Share of Linnaeus University's 2011–2017 graduates living in Kalmar County in 2017
examinerade_bor_i_kalmar_lan_2017.note: A further 27% lived in Kronoberg County, so 53% lived in the Linnaeus region; among other counties Stockholm (11%) and Skåne (9%) were the largest. Of those born outside the region 36% stayed, against 83% of those born in Kalmar or Kronoberg County (STATIV 2017).

hogskoleutbildade_med_lnu_examen.name: Share of university graduates established in Kalmar and Växjö who hold a Linnaeus University degree
hogskoleutbildade_med_lnu_examen.note: The figure in the 2024 annual report comes from an unpublished internal report (Studentrekrytering, etableringsmönster och kompetensförsörjning, 2023) and covers Kalmar and Växjö together. The vice-chancellor also states that 80% of applicants from the region stay in the regional labour market, against 20% of those who come from elsewhere.

studentbostader_kalmarhem.name: Student homes in Kalmarhem's housing stock
studentbostader_kalmarhem.note: Down from 984 the year before; Kalmarhem describes falling demand for student housing over several years and has adjusted its supply. Through the student housing guarantee (newly admitted students who register as residents of Kalmar are offered a student home), 428 contracts were signed in 2024 against 386 in 2021, and annual turnover in the student stock is 63%. Kalmar was named Student City of the Year 2023 by the Swedish National Union of Students (Linnaeus University annual report 2024).

lnu_kostnader_kalmar_uppskattning.name: Linnaeus University's annual spending in Kalmar (estimate)
lnu_kostnader_kalmar_uppskattning.note: Own estimate: 36–40% of the university's total costs of SEK 2,504 million in 2025, of which 68% is staff and 12% premises. This is gross spending, not a calculated regional impact; no study of the university's economic importance for Kalmar has been found.

lnu_resultat_mnkr.name: Linnaeus University's annual result (change in capital), whole university
lnu_resultat_mnkr.note: The second deficit in a row after −SEK 95 million in 2024 (+SEK 28 million in 2023), and agency capital has fallen from SEK 383 million to SEK 221 million. The vice-chancellor points to reduced government funding; the education funding ceiling is being lowered for 2025–2027 while student numbers rose in 2025, so the university delivered 104% of its ceiling (UKÄ).

lnu_sparkrav_mnkr.name: Linnaeus University's savings requirement 2027–2029
lnu_sparkrav_mnkr.note: In June 2026 the university board decided on savings of about SEK 120 million, including SEK 50 million in support functions in 2027–2028, after staffing had been cut by 30 full-time equivalents in 2025; a hiring freeze in the administration applies from 18 May 2026 to 30 June 2027. According to the Saco-S union the changes are under way in both Kalmar and Växjö, with no faculty hit especially hard (Universitetsläraren, 2026-09-21). In March 2026 the vice-chancellor said the university may have a thousand fewer students and that its range of courses and programmes is to shrink by 15% by 2030, mainly distance learning (SVT).

unga_19_24_kalmar_prognos_2050.name: Residents aged 19–24 in Kalmar Municipality in 2050 according to Statistics Sweden's projection
unga_19_24_kalmar_prognos_2050.note: Sum of single-year ages 19–24, both sexes (own summation): 5,851 (2025), peaking at 6,688 (2035), 5,730 (2050) and 6,560 (2070). The 19–24 share is 8.0% in Kalmar Municipality in 2025 against 7.0% for Sweden as a whole and 5.9% for the county (own calculations), a university-town effect. The projection assumes that today's migration patterns, and with them the university, continue.

unga_19_24_sverige_prognos_2050.name: Residents aged 19–24 in Sweden in 2050 according to Statistics Sweden's population projection
unga_19_24_sverige_prognos_2050.note: Sum of single-year ages 19–24 (own summation): 740,827 (2026), peaking at 779,316 (2035) and 667,595 (2050), i.e. −14% from the peak and −10% compared with 2026 (own calculations). Higher education's natural recruitment base grows until the mid-2030s and then shrinks, which sharpens competition for students.

olandsbron_livslangd_planerad_till.name: Planned service life of Ölandsbron (at least until year)
olandsbron_livslangd_planerad_till.note: Trafikverket's bridge manager in 2022: the bridge "shall last until at least 2075, unless there are major changes in how we live or travel", and the intention is a total life of at least 100 years from the 1972 opening. Parliamentary motion 2025/26:3712 confirms that Trafikverket plans for 2075, and the 2026–2030 renovation is meant to extend the bridge's life.

olandsbron_renovering_2027_2030_mnkr.name: Contract value for the 2027–2030 concrete renovation of Ölandsbron
olandsbron_renovering_2027_2030_mnkr.note: NCC's winning bid (W-Tech bid 787.5 MSEK) to restore and thicken the concrete cover on the main and cross beams of 135 spans, January 2027–June 2030, after a 2025 pilot covering 13 spans. Trafikverket is also replacing the expansion joints from August 2026 to March 2027, with one lane closed in each direction. The bridge cost 130 MSEK to build.

olandsbron_segelfri_hojd_m.name: Navigation clearance under the high span of Ölandsbron
olandsbron_segelfri_hojd_m.note: The bridge is 6,072 m long, built of reinforced concrete in 155 spans, and reaches a maximum height of 41.69 m (Dagens PS 2026). The clearance governs shipping through Kalmarsund and the gradient of any future replacement bridge.

olandsbron_bredd_m.name: Width of Ölandsbron between the edge beams
olandsbron_bredd_m.note: The deck is divided into four lanes with 0.2 m shoulders and has no footpath or cycle lane. The speed limit varies between 50 and 90 km/h. A tram, bus or cycle lane fits only if car traffic loses lanes or a new bridge is built.

olandsbron_adt_2009.name: Annual average daily traffic on Ölandsbron in 2009
olandsbron_adt_2009.note: The most recent exact annual average found in an official source. Trafikverket now gives rounded figures of about 15,000 vehicles a day outside summer and 25,000 in summer (see olandsbron_fordon_per_dygn). Motion 2025/26:3712 gives nearly 7 million vehicles a year, about 19,000 a day.

olandsbron_fordon_toppdygn.name: Traffic on Ölandsbron on peak days (Öland harvest festival)
olandsbron_fordon_toppdygn.note: During the harvest festival on the last weekend of September, up to 36,000 vehicles can cross per day, compared with an average of 25,000 in summer and 15,000 the rest of the year. The peak days set the length of the queues at the bridgeheads in Färjestaden and Kalmar.

olandsbron_vind_avradan_ms.name: Wind speed at which wind-sensitive vehicles are advised not to cross Ölandsbron
olandsbron_vind_avradan_ms.note: "Already at 27 metres per second we advise wind-sensitive vehicles not to cross"; trailers have overturned in strong winds. Since 14 May 2018, Trafikverket rather than the police closes the bridge with red lights and barriers, and traffic is turned back at Svinö and Färjestaden.

olandsbron_vind_stangning_ms.name: Wind speed at which Ölandsbron is closed to all traffic
olandsbron_vind_stangning_ms.note: "If there is a hurricane and the wind blows at 32 metres per second, the bridge is closed." Trafikverket describes wind closures as "isolated occasions". No official count of closure days per year has been found.

olandsbron_gang_cykelforbud_sedan.name: Walking and cycling on Ölandsbron banned since
olandsbron_gang_cykelforbud_sedan.note: The county administrative board decided the ban on 17 December 2009. Transportstyrelsen rejected the appeal by Cykelfrämjandet and Kalmar miljögrupp on 21 June 2010, citing four lanes, high speeds and 0.2 m shoulders. Today's alternatives are taking a bike on the regional bus, space permitting, and the seasonal bicycle ferry.

olandsleden_tallhagen_lagsta_niva.name: Lowest ground level on road 137 (Ölandsleden) between Ölandsbron and the mainland, Tallhagen
olandsleden_tallhagen_lagsta_niva.note: Own derived value: the 1.09 m water depth at the +3.4 m level gives a ground level of 2.31 m, and the coastal flood layers give "wet from" 2.4 m. About 440 m of the road, 1.0–1.4 km west of the bridgehead on Svinö, lies below 3.4 m. The road clears the model's 2126 100-year levels (1.89–2.18 m) by 0.1–0.4 m but is under 0.4 m of water at the 2150 level of 2.7 m (SSP2-4.5). The Öland side at Möllstorp lies above 3.4 m.

olandsbron_reservfarja_ledtid.name: Time needed to get a replacement ferry in place if Ölandsbron is closed (figure from a parliamentary question)
olandsbron_reservfarja_ledtid.note: According to the MP asking the question (also question 2022/23:131), it can take up to two weeks to reclassify Trafikverket's road ferry and move it from the Blekinge archipelago to Kalmarsund. He wants a maximum of 24 hours. The government's answers of 13 December 2022 and 24 February 2026 do not confirm the figure but refer to Trafikverket's continuity planning. There is no permanent backup link for cars.

olandsbron_bargning_installelsetid.name: Permitted response time for contracted recovery (towing) services on Ölandsbron
olandsbron_bargning_installelsetid.note: The figure was given in a parliamentary question after at least two accidents in winter 2025/26 caused long queues across the bridge. On 24 February 2026, the infrastructure minister replied that Trafikverket is analysing whether its routines and contract requirements need to change.

oland_arbetspendlare_till_kalmar.name: Employed residents of Öland whose workplace is in Kalmar Municipality (Öland)
oland_arbetspendlare_till_kalmar.note: The sum of Mörbylånga (2,988) and Borgholm (779) from SCB register data for 2024. A further 1,017 Öland residents work in other mainland municipalities, and 2,077 mainland residents (1,537 of them in Kalmar) work on Öland, so in total about 6,860 people commute across the strait. The register records the workplace, not that the trip is made every day.

morbylanga_utpendling_andel.name: Share of employed residents of Mörbylånga Municipality who commute to another municipality (Öland)
morbylanga_utpendling_andel.note: The highest share in the county, and rising (51.3% in 2020). Borgholm had 28.9% and Kalmar 20.1% in 2024. Most out-commuters from Mörbylånga work in Kalmar and so depend on Ölandsbron.

cykelfarja_cyklar_per_sasong.name: Bicycles carried by the Kalmar–Färjestaden bicycle ferry per season (Öland)
cykelfarja_cyklar_per_sasong.note: The requirement in the municipalities' direct procurement of the service from 2026: the operator must handle just over 40,000 passengers and 13,000 bicycles per season. Trafikverket's support of 1.4 MSEK a year has ended, and Kalmar and Mörbylånga contribute about 100,000 SEK each.

kalmar_c_tagrorelser_per_dygn.name: Train movements to and from Kalmar C per day
kalmar_c_tagrorelser_per_dygn.note: "Just under 70 train movements", meaning just over 30 departures a day. Kalmar C is a terminus with three platform tracks for trains of at most 250 m. In rush hour, the barriers at the three level crossings on the single track towards Kalmar södra are down for up to 20 minutes an hour.

kalmar_c_ombyggnad_mnkr.name: Investment cost of a new island platform and new platform tracks at Kalmar C
kalmar_c_ombyggnad_mnkr.note: A new island platform, new platform tracks 6–7 and a longer platform for longer trains. The project is in the national plan adopted on 24 April 2026, but only under "planning", with no construction start decided. The rebuilding of Emmaboda station was dropped from the plan.

kalmar_c_resor_prognos_2045.name: Forecast of train trips to and from Kalmar C in 2045
kalmar_c_resor_prognos_2045.note: Trafikverket's base forecast for 2045: 80 passenger trains a day and 1.4 million trips a year on the track into Kalmar C. None of the sources found gives today's passenger numbers at Kalmar C.

oresundstag_avgangar_kalmar_vardag.name: Direct Öresundståg trains from Kalmar C towards Malmö/Copenhagen per weekday
oresundstag_avgangar_kalmar_vardag.note: Own count from the timetable: departures from Kalmar between 06:00 and 21:00, Monday to Friday, most of them running through to Østerport. Krösatåg trains also run Kalmar–Emmaboda–Karlskrona/Växjö and Kalmar–Linköping, and SJ runs towards Alvesta and Gothenburg.

restid_tag_kalmar_kobenhavn_min.name: Fastest train journey time Kalmar C–København H
restid_tag_kalmar_kobenhavn_min.note: Direct Öresundståg train with no change, for example departing 06:00 and arriving 09:44. The journey to Copenhagen Airport takes 3 h 28 min. All through trains during the day have the same running time.

restid_tag_kalmar_malmo_min.name: Fastest train journey time Kalmar C–Malmö C
restid_tag_kalmar_malmo_min.note: Öresundståg train from Kalmar at 06:00 to Malmö C at 09:03, via Växjö, Alvesta, Hässleholm and Lund. The Hässleholm–Lund project (two new tracks) is in the 2026–2037 national plan and, according to SVT, will improve train services between Kalmar and Malmö/Copenhagen.

restid_tag_kalmar_vaxjo_min.name: Fastest train journey time Kalmar C–Växjö
restid_tag_kalmar_vaxjo_min.note: Öresundståg train stopping at Nybro, Emmaboda, Lessebo and Hovmantorp. The Kust till kust line is electrified but single-track. The target of Regionsamverkan Sydsverige is 45 minutes by 2040 (see restid_mal_kalmar_vaxjo_2040).

restid_tag_kalmar_linkoping_min.name: Fastest train journey time Kalmar C–Linköping (Stångådalsbanan)
restid_tag_kalmar_linkoping_min.note: Krösatåg train from Kalmar at 10:35 to Linköping at 13:40 in the 2024 timetable. The trip is up to 20 minutes shorter via Alvesta and the Southern Main Line. The 1990s upgrade cut the journey from about four hours to three.

restid_tag_kalmar_stockholm_min.name: Approximate fastest train journey time Kalmar C–Stockholm C (with a change)
restid_tag_kalmar_stockholm_min.note: Derived: Trafikverket states that Kalmar–Stockholm is 20–30 minutes faster via Alvesta than via Linköping. Kalmar–Linköping (3 h 05) plus a change and SJ's roughly 1 h 40 for Linköping–Stockholm (an assumption) gives about 4 h 55–5 h 05, so about 4 h 30–4 h 45 via Alvesta (Kalmar–Alvesta takes 1 h 20 on Öresundståg). There are no direct trains; the direct trains via Linköping ended after 2003.

stangadalsbanan_elektrifierad_andel.name: Electrified share of Stångådalsbanan, Kalmar–Linköping
stangadalsbanan_elektrifierad_andel.note: The line is 235 km long, single-track and has no overhead wire. In 2024, Trafikverket proposed neither overhead wire nor partial electrification. The Kust till kust line Kalmar–Emmaboda–Alvesta, by contrast, is electrified. Eight new bimodal Krösatåg trains (electric and biodiesel), delivered from 2026–2027, are to make fossil-free operation possible.

stangadalsbanan_resor_per_ar.name: Trips per year on Stångådalsbanan
stangadalsbanan_resor_per_ar.note: "Just under 340,000" trips in 2018, just over 230,000 in 2020 and just over 180,000 in 2021. Ridership has been flat since around 2000. Kalmar C is part of 45% of the trips on the line, and Kalmar–Linköping is the largest single pair (14%).

stangadalsbanan_genomgaende_turer.name: Through trains Kalmar–Linköping per weekday
stangadalsbanan_genomgaende_turer.note: Seven through return trips in the 2024 timetable plus some split services, about 23 passenger trains a day on the line in total (Trafikverket 2024). Collisions with fallen trees are increasing: 37 cases in 2018–2022 and 30 in 2023 alone.

stangadalsbanan_atgarder_2022_2033_mnkr.name: Decided state measures on Stångådalsbanan and Tjustbanan 2022–2033
stangadalsbanan_atgarder_2022_2033_mnkr.note: "Just over 2.2 billion SEK", about half of it routine maintenance. A new radio-block signalling system costs about 800 MSEK. A triangle junction at Berga and a passing loop at Kåremo would cut Kalmar–Linköping by just under 10 minutes.

restid_mal_kalmar_vaxjo_2040.name: Target train journey time Kalmar–Växjö by 2040 (Regionsamverkan Sydsverige)
restid_mal_kalmar_vaxjo_2040.note: Down from 60 minutes in 2018. The same position paper aims to cut Kalmar–Karlskrona from 75 to 60 minutes. Region Kalmar wants double track Kalmar–Alvesta in the long run, but double track Växjö–Alvesta is not in the 2026–2037 national plan.

kollektivtrafik_marknadsandel_mal_2028.name: Target public transport share of motorised trips in the county by 2028
kollektivtrafik_marknadsandel_mal_2028.note: The share was 12% in 2022 (14% before the pandemic) and 21% in Kalmar Municipality. The number of trips is also to rise above the 2019 level; in 2022 there were almost 10 million trips on subsidised public transport.

lansplan_kalmar_2026_2037_mnkr.name: Financial frame for the regional transport infrastructure plan for Kalmar County 2026–2037
lansplan_kalmar_2026_2037_mnkr.note: Out of a national frame of 1,171 billion SEK; according to SVT, 307 MSEK more than the previous period. Ölandsbron, a second link to Öland and electrification of Stångådalsbanan are not named projects in the national plan.

flyg_passagerare_kalmar_2025.name: Passengers at Kalmar Öland Airport in 2025
flyg_passagerare_kalmar_2025.note: Down 1.3% on 2024 and 38% of the 2019 level. The second quarter of 2026 was 13% below the year before. The only scheduled route is SAS to Arlanda (no Bromma route since January 2025), plus charter flights. The airport is owned half by Kalmar Municipality and half by Region Kalmar län.

flyg_passagerare_kalmar_2019.name: Passengers at Kalmar Öland Airport in 2019
flyg_passagerare_kalmar_2019.note: Down 4.6% from 243,296 passengers in 2018. This is the pre-pandemic level, when there were routes to both Arlanda and Bromma.

flyg_co2_inrikes_kalmar_2024.name: Carbon dioxide from domestic aviation allocated to Kalmar Municipality
flyg_co2_inrikes_kalmar_2024.note: Emissions were 1,636 tonnes in 1990, 1,001 tonnes in 2015 and 686 tonnes in 2023. The value covers only the part of emissions that the database allocates geographically to the municipality, mainly take-off and landing near the airport, not the whole flights. International charter flights are reported as 0.

vattenbrist_och_torka.title: Water shortages and recurring drought
vattenbrist_och_torka.text: Kalmar County is one of Sweden's most water-stressed counties. In 2016, groundwater in south-eastern Sweden was at its lowest since measurements began, and Öland received drinking water by tanker truck and via a pipeline across the Kalmar Strait. The County Administrative Board counts 2016, 2018 and 2022 as drought years, and in September 2026 groundwater levels in both small and large aquifers were unusually low across almost the entire county. Agriculture accounts for 19% of the county's freshwater use (Sweden as a whole 3%), and SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) projects 30–50 days of low soil moisture per year by the end of the century.

overgodning_kalmarsund.title: Eutrophication in the Kalmar Strait and the Baltic Sea
overgodning_kalmarsund.text: No coastal water body in Kalmar Municipality or the county has good ecological status, and none of the county's 21 coastal stations has had good nutrient status in eight years – all stations in the Kalmar area are unsatisfactory, mainly because of phosphorus. Eelgrass in the Kalmar Strait is declining. According to HELCOM, phosphorus inputs to the Baltic Sea have fallen by 28% since 1997–2003, but with no visible recovery in 2016–2021, and 93.8% of the Baltic Sea is still below good status for eutrophication (HELCOM HOLAS 3). The deadline for good status in Kalmar's coastal waters is 2039.

havsniva_kvarnholmen.title: Rising seas threaten Kvarnholmen and the city centre
havsniva_kvarnholmen.text: SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) calculates that mean sea level in Kalmar will rise by 47 cm (SSP2-4.5) to 68 cm (SSP5-8.5) by 2100 despite land uplift, and by about 0.9 m by 2126 in the high scenario. The city of Kalmar is one of the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency's (MSB) areas with significant flood risk: the station area, large parts of Kvarnholmen, Ängö, Varvsholmen and Tjärhovet are under threat, several quays have poor structural strength and the port can only cope with about 70 cm of permanent rise. New buildings must withstand +2.8 m RH2000.

bilberoende_transportutslapp.title: Car dependence and transport emissions
bilberoende_transportutslapp.text: Transport accounts for 47% of the municipality's territorial emissions, and in 2024 emissions rose for the first time in almost 20 years when the emissions reduction obligation for fuels was lowered. The car accounts for about 60% of trips, and there are 498 passenger cars per 1,000 inhabitants. The municipality's climate contract aims for emissions 85% below 1990 levels by 2030, but in 2024 the reduction was 45%.

jordbrukets_utslapp_och_lackage.title: Agricultural climate emissions and nutrient leaching
jordbrukets_utslapp_och_lackage.text: Agriculture is the county's largest source of emissions (about 40%, 2.10 t CO2e per inhabitant versus 0.58 in Sweden as a whole), and its emissions have increased slightly since 1990, while they have fallen nationally. Livestock digestion accounts for 57% of agricultural emissions. Only 5.9% of the arable land in Kalmar Municipality is farmed organically (Sweden as a whole 14%), and nutrient leaching from farmland is a main cause of eutrophication.

aldrande_lan_och_avfolkning.title: An ageing, shrinking county around a growing main town
aldrande_lan_och_avfolkning.text: Kalmar Municipality is growing (+3.9% in five years) while Kalmar County is shrinking (−875 people in 2025) and has 26.7% of its inhabitants over 65. In Kalmar Municipality, the number of people aged 80+ rose by 5.8% in a single year. Rural agriculture is ageing too: 60% of the county's farmers are over 54, and the number of agricultural businesses has fallen by 23% since 2010.

livsmedelsberedskap_importberoende.title: Vulnerable food preparedness and import dependence
livsmedelsberedskap_importberoende.text: Sweden has no overall self-sufficiency rate; dairy is at 75% and fresh tomatoes at 19%, and production relies on imported fertiliser, feed, fuel and machinery. Government emergency stockpiles are being built up from virtually zero, starting in 2026. Region Kalmar County itself points out that there is no storage of the county's own production and that the Öland Bridge is a particular risk. Only 36% of Swedes have drinks at home for a week.

psykisk_ohalsa_och_isolering.title: Mental ill health and social isolation
psykisk_ohalsa_och_isolering.text: The share of adults in Kalmar Municipality with serious psychological distress rose from 7.9% to 11.0% between two survey periods, and 8.4% of children and young people have a psychiatric diagnosis, psychiatric care or psychotropic medication – a rising trend. In the county, the share with low social participation has risen from 18% to 37.9%. 87% of 13–16-year-olds in Sweden have more than three hours of screen time per day.

tillit_trygghet_segregation.title: Low trust, insecurity and residential segregation
tillit_trygghet_segregation.text: 33.9% of inhabitants in Kalmar Municipality lack trust in others (Sweden as a whole 29.6%), and 31% feel unsafe outdoors late in the evening in their own neighbourhood (Sweden as a whole 25%). Boverket (National Board of Housing, Building and Planning) classifies Norrliden as an area with major socio-economic challenges, while Berga has very good conditions.

bostadsbyggandet_har_stannat.title: Housing construction has slowed
bostadsbyggandet_har_stannat.text: In 2025, only 0.96 dwellings per 1,000 inhabitants were completed in Kalmar Municipality, compared with 3.1 in Sweden as a whole. The municipality reports a housing shortage now and in three years' time, particularly of large, affordable and senior housing, and expects about 160 housing starts in 2026. High construction costs, lending conditions and appeals are holding construction back.

lite_skyddad_natur.title: Little protected nature and threatened biodiversity
lite_skyddad_natur.text: Only 1.0% of the municipality's land area is protected (Sweden as a whole 12.6%), and 2.2% of the total area including sea. The eelgrass meadows in the Kalmar Strait are declining. The municipality's first municipal nature reserve (Stensö) is to be established in 2026.

varme_och_klimatstress.title: Heatwaves in an ageing city
varme_och_klimatstress.text: SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) expects the mean annual temperature in the county to rise by 1.7, 2.8 or 4.6 °C by 2071–2100 compared with 1971–2000, depending on emissions (RCP2.6, 4.5, 8.5). Days above 25 °C rise to 27–57 a year from about 15 today, and the longest spell of high-summer heat grows to 22 days with high emissions. Kalmar has already become 1.1 °C warmer between the normal periods 1961–1990 and 1991–2020. Tree canopy covers only about 22% of the Kalmar urban area, against the municipality's benchmark of 30%, while the number of inhabitants over 80 is rising rapidly.

hog_solinstralning.title: Sweden's sunshine coast
hog_solinstralning.text: Kalmar receives about 1,136 kWh/m² of solar irradiation per year (SMHI model, mean 2015–2024), about 9% more than Stockholm and 50% more than Kiruna. The municipality has 47 MW of solar PV (about 650 W per inhabitant versus about 520 in Sweden as a whole), and Kalmar Energi's member-owned Törneby solar park was the largest of its kind in Sweden when it was built in 2017.

fornybar_fjarrvarme_moskogen.title: Almost entirely renewable district heating and combined heat and power
fornybar_fjarrvarme_moskogen.text: 99.4% of the district heating in the municipality is renewable. Kalmar Energi's Moskogen combined heat and power plant (2009) is fuelled by forest wood chips, bark and by-products, produces 360 GWh of heat and about 130 GWh of electricity per year (roughly a third of Kalmar's electricity needs) and has a heat store of 21,600 m³. Kalmar Energi is investigating bio-CCUS at Moskogen, which could deliver negative emissions.

tidiga_fossilmal.title: Early fossil-free targets and climate contracts
tidiga_fossilmal.text: The county has had the goal of becoming a fossil-fuel-free region by 2030 since 2006, and the municipality has had the goal of a fossil-fuel-free municipality by 2030 in its operational plans since 2008. The municipality's territorial emissions have fallen by 45% since 1990 (7.1 → 3.0 t per inhabitant). Kalmar is one of 23 municipalities in Viable Cities' Climate Neutral Cities 2030, and 25 local businesses signed climate contracts with the municipality in 2024.

havsvindkraft_kalmarsund.title: A pioneer in offshore wind power
havsvindkraft_kalmarsund.text: The Utgrunden offshore wind farm near Öland was built as early as 2000 (7 turbines of 1.5 MW each, 10.5 MW) and was dismantled in 2018 when the turbines reached the end of their service life. Kårehamn, east of Öland (16 turbines, 48 MW), has produced about 194 GWh/year since 2013. Within Kalmar Municipality there are 31 wind turbines (81 MW), which generated 191 GWh in 2024.

biogas_fossilfri_kollektivtrafik.title: Local biogas and fossil-free public transport
biogas_fossilfri_kollektivtrafik.text: All Kalmar Länstrafik buses are fossil-free and run on biogas and HVO, and most of the biogas is produced within the county; biogas accounted for 59% of the energy in the county's public transport in 2022. More Biogas, north of Kalmar, has been making vehicle gas from manure and food waste since 2014 and is partly owned by farmers. Two large new biogas plants are planned in the southern part of the municipality.

starkt_livsmedelslan.title: One of Sweden's strongest food-producing counties
starkt_livsmedelslan.text: Kalmar County has 2.3% of the population but 20% of Sweden's chicken production, 12% of its milk and eggs and 10% of its beef, and is a net exporter of food.
